node.title: Mitochondrial permeability transition
node.canonical_question: What is mitochondrial permeability transition and when does it occur?
node.summary: Mitochondrial permeability transition (mPT) is a sudden, large-scale opening of a pore in the inner mitochondrial membrane during stress. The pore allows molecules up to about 1.5 kDa to flood in, collapsing the proton gradient and causing the mitochondrion to swell, halting ATP synthesis and often triggering cell death.

sections.title: What mitochondrial permeability transition is
sections.content: Under normal conditions, the inner mitochondrial membrane is highly selective — it keeps most ions out so that the proton gradient can be maintained for ATP synthesis. Mitochondrial permeability transition (mPT) is when this selectivity suddenly breaks down. A large pore called the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opens in the inner membrane, making it suddenly permeable to molecules up to about 1.5 kilodaltons. This is a dramatic reversal of the usual tight control.

sections.title: Consequences of pore opening
sections.content: When the mPTP opens, small molecules and ions rush across the inner membrane down their concentration gradients. The proton gradient collapses instantly, so ATP synthase can no longer make ATP. Osmotic pressure builds inside the mitochondrial matrix as solutes flood in, causing the matrix to swell. This swelling can rupture the outer mitochondrial membrane. Rupture releases cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic proteins into the cytoplasm, which activate the cell's internal death programme (apoptosis). If many mitochondria in the same cell undergo mPT at once, the rapid ATP loss can also trigger necrosis.

sections.title: When mPT occurs — the triggers
sections.content: mPTP opening is triggered by conditions that indicate severe cellular stress. The main triggers are: (1) calcium overload — high calcium concentration in the mitochondrial matrix is the primary stimulus; (2) oxidative stress — excess reactive oxygen species damage the pore components; (3) loss of the proton gradient — if the membrane potential falls sharply, the pore is more likely to open; (4) prolonged opening of the mPT is promoted by high inorganic phosphate and adenine nucleotide depletion. mPT is therefore most relevant in pathological situations such as ischaemia-reperfusion injury (for example, when blood flow returns to a heart after a heart attack) and in neurodegenerative diseases where mitochondrial calcium handling is impaired.

sections.title: The molecular identity of the mPTP
sections.content: The exact molecular composition of the mPTP has been debated for decades. Current evidence points to the F-ATP synthase (the same enzyme that normally makes ATP) as a core structural component of the pore, with the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT) and cyclophilin D (a matrix protein) as regulators. Cyclophilin D is important because the immunosuppressant drug cyclosporin A inhibits it and thereby reduces mPT opening — this has been tested in experiments to limit reperfusion injury.

sections.title: Connection to the main lesson
sections.content: Under healthy conditions the inner membrane's impermeability is essential for ATP production (as covered in the parent lesson on mitochondrial energy production). mPT is the breakdown of that impermeability under extreme stress. It connects the membrane structure, the proton gradient, the electron transport chain, and cytochrome c release — all topics from this course — but as a failure mode rather than a normal function.

rendering.explanation: The inner mitochondrial membrane is normally almost impermeable, which is what lets the proton gradient build up and drive ATP synthesis. Mitochondrial permeability transition is what happens when that barrier suddenly gives way under stress. A large pore opens up, the gradient collapses, the mitochondrion swells, and the cell often dies as a result. The two biggest triggers are a flood of calcium ions into the mitochondrion and a surge of damaging reactive oxygen species. This is most relevant in situations like a heart attack, where a burst of calcium and oxidative stress after blood flow returns can kill heart cells through this mechanism.
